We present baseline steatosis prevalence and cardiometabolic characteristics among REPRIEVE substudy participants.Methods:REPRIEVE is an international, primary cardiovascular disease prevention, randomized, controlled trial of pitavastatin calcium vs. placebo among 7769 PWH ages 40-75years on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and with low-To-moderate cardiovascular risk. A subset of participants underwent noncontrast computed tomography, with hepatic steatosis defined as mean hepatic attenuation less than 40 HU or liver/spleen ratio less than 1.0, and NAFLD defined as steatosis in the absence of frequent alcohol use or viral hepatitis.Results:Of 687 evaluable persons, median age was 51years, BMI 27kg/m2, CD4+T-cell count 607 cells/μl; 17% natal female sex, 36% Black, 24% Hispanic, and 98% HIV-1 RNA less than 400copies/ml. Hepatic steatosis prevalence was 22% (149/687), and NAFLD 21% (96/466). Steatosis/NAFLD prevalence was higher in men and with older age, non-Black race, and higher BMI and waist circumference. Both were associated with BMI greater than 30kg/m2, metabolic syndrome components, higher atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk score, HOMA-IR, LpPLA-2 and hs-CRP, and lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Of HIV-specific/ART-specific characteristics, only history of an AIDS-defining illness was more common among persons with steatosis/NAFLD. After adjusting for age, sex and race/ethnicity, BMI greater than 30kg/m2, HOMA-IR greater than 2.0, Metabolic syndrome and each of its components were associated with NAFLD prevalence.Conclusion:In this cohort with controlled HIV and low-To-moderate cardiovascular risk, hepatic steatosis and NAFLD were common and associated with clinically relevant metabolic and inflammatory disturbances but not current HIV-related or ART-related factors.

title: Correction to: Etripamil Nasal Spray: Therapeutic Potential for Treating Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (American Journal of Cardiovascular Drugs, (2023), 23, 5, (471-475), 10.1007/s40256-023-00589-2)
abstract: In this article, few statements were published incorrectly and the correct details are provided below. Section 1, lines 7 to 13 currently reads as “Those at risk for arrythmias include patients with genetic dispositions, obesity, extreme endurance exercises, and excessive alcohol and tobacco consumption. Other common risk factors include coronary artery disease, hypertension, cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease [4]. Without proper treatment, complications can lead to myocardial infarction, angina, or even stroke.” It should have read “Those at risk for arrythmias include patients with chronic lung disease, hyperthyroidism, cardiomyopathies, and structural heart disease [4]. Without proper treatment, complications can lead to loss of consciousness, heart failure, or cardiac arrest.” Section 1, line 22 currently reads as “to these limitations, drug delivery via the pulmonary route” and should have read “to these limitations, drug delivery via the intranasal route” Section 1, lines 26–28 currently reads as “Compared with oral medications, pulmonary drug delivery averts first-pass metabolism and any associated toxicities typical of orally administered” and should have read “Compared with oral medications, intranasal drug delivery averts first-pass metabolism and any associated toxicities typical of orally administered” Section 1, lines 29–32 currently reads as “CCBs. In addition, the lungs’ expansive surface area and thin vasculature for drug absorption allow for an efficient route for delivering etripamil to patients at a low dose without intensive and invasive care [4].” It should have read “In addition, absorption in the nasal mucosa allows for an efficient route for delivering etripamil to patients at a low dose without intensive and invasive care.” Section 1.2, lines 7–9 currently reads as “The concentration plateaus at a 70 mg dose, as further drug delivery after this dose does not result in a higher effective concentration.” It should have read “The plasma concentration plateaus at a 70 mg dose, as further drug delivery after this dose does not result in a higher conversion.” Section 1.2, lines 14–15 currently reads as “This effect occurs approximately three minutes after inhalation.” It should have read “This effect occurs approximately three minutes after intranasal administration.” Section 2, lines 53–61 currently reads as “The RAPID study is composed of four arms, two of which consist of patients enrolled during part 1, randomized 2:1 to a single dose of study drug (etripamil nasal spray 70 mg or placebo) to treat a perceived episode of PSVT. The other two arms consist of newly enrolled patients who passed a test dose regimen of etripamil nasal spray 70 mg, randomized 1:1 to a dosing regimen of etripamil or placebo that allowed patients to self-administer a second dose to treat a perceived PSVT episode [13].” It should have read “The RAPID study comprised two arms: etripamil and placebo. The RAPID study population consists of 34 patients enrolled during Part 1 of NODE-301 who did not have a PSVT episode by the cut-off date and 658 newly enrolled patients who passed a test dose regimen of etripamil nasal spray 70 mg, randomized 1:1 to a dosing regimen of etripamil or placebo that allows patients to self-administer a second dose to treat a perceived PSVT episode [14].” Section 2.1, lines 26–31 currently reads as “In the phase III study NODE-303, patient self-administration of etripamil 70 mg nasal spray during episodes of PSVT after the failure of vagal maneuver to terminate the NODE-301, patient self-administration of etripamil 70 mg nasal spray during episodes of PSVT after the failure of vagal maneuver to terminate the arrhythmia resulted in first degree atrioventricular heart block lasting greater than 30 seconds in eight subjects in the etripamil 70 mg group, with otherwise no difference in safety between etripamil and placebo [16].” Section 3, lines 1–2 currently reads as “Self-administered shorting-acting treatment for patients with” and should have read “Self-administered, short-acting treatment for patients with” Section 3, lines 3–5 currently reads as the only available relief option is IV treatment with calcium channel blockers or adenosine administered in a professional medical setting.” Section 3, lines 8–11 currently reads as “Episodic treatment may provide the additional benefit of allowing patients to halt chronic prophylactic therapy with beta blockers and CCBs [15].” It should have read “Episodic treatment may provide the title: Diagnosis and Management of Osteoporosis: A Comprehensive Review of Guidelines
abstract: Importance Osteoporosis causes increased morbidity and mortality, and thus poses a significant economic burden to the health systems worldwide. Objective The aim of this study was to review and compare the most recently published major guidelines on diagnosis and management of this common medical entity. Evidence Acquisition A thorough comparative review of the most influential guidelines from the RACGP (Royal Australian College of General Practitioners), the ESCEO-IOF (European Society for Clinical and Economic Aspects of Osteoporosis-International Osteoporosis Foundation), the NOGG (National Osteoporosis Guideline Group), the NAMS (North American Menopause Society), the ES (Endocrine Society), and the ACOG (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists) was conducted. Results The reviewed guidelines generally agree on the definition, the criteria, and investigations used to diagnose osteoporosis. They also concur regarding the risk factors for osteoporosis and the suggested lifestyle modifications (calcium and vitamin D intake, normal body weight, reduction of alcohol consumption, and smoking cessation). However, there is lack of consensus on indications for fracture risk assessment in the general population and the exact indications for bone mineral density assessment. Referral to a bone specialist is reserved for complex cases of osteoporosis (NOGG, NAMS, and ACOG) or in case of inadequate access to care (RACGP). The use of hip protectors to reduce the risk of fractures is supported by RACGP, NOGG, and NAMS, solely for high-risk elderly patients in residential care settings. All guidelines reviewed recognize the efficacy of the pharmacologic agents (ie, bisphosphonates, denosumab, hormone therapy, and parathyroid hormone analogs). Nonetheless, recommendations regarding monitoring of pharmacotherapy differ, primarily in the case of bisphosphonates. The proposed intervals of repeat bone mineral density testing after initiation of drug therapy are set at 2 years (RACGP), 1-3 years (NAMS, ES, and ACOG), or 3-5 years (ESCEO-IOF and NOGG). All guidelines agree upon the restricted use of bone turnover markers only in bone specialist centers for treatment monitoring purposes. Finally, the definition of treatment failure varies among the reviewed guidelines. Conclusions Osteoporosis is a distressing condition for women, mainly those of postmenopausal age. Thus, it seems of paramount importance to develop consistent international practice protocols for more cost-effective diagnostic and management techniques, in order to improve women's quality of life. Target Audience Obstetricians and gynecologists, family physicians. Learning Objectives After participating in this activity, the physician should be able to identify early risk factors for osteoporosis; describe the appropriate diagnostic techniques for osteoporosis; and explain available drug agents for the management of osteoporosis, as well as the difference in approach regarding their use.

title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter type 2 inhibitors and cardiac arrhythmias
abstract: The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors as a new and effective class of therapeutic agents for type 2 diabetes (T2D) preventing the reabsorption of glucose in the kidneys and thus facilitating glucose excretion in the urine, but also as agents with cardiovascular benefits, particularly in patients with heart failure (HF), regardless of the diabetic status, has ushered in a new era in treating patients with T2D and/or HF. In addition, data have recently emerged indicating an antiarrhythmic effect of the SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with and without diabetes. Prospective studies, randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have provided robust evidence for a protective and beneficial effect of these agents against atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The antiarrhythmic mechanisms involved include reverse atrial and ventricular remodeling, amelioration of mitochondrial function, reduction of hypoglycemic episodes with their attendant arrhythmogenic effects, attenuated sympathetic nervous system activity, regulation of sodium and calcium homeostasis, and suppression of prolonged ventricular repolarization. These new data on antiarrhythmic actions of SGLT2 inhibitors are herein reviewed, potential mechanisms involved are discussed and pictorially illustrated, and treatment results on specific arrhythmias are described and tabulated.

title: LAMBERT-EATON: A RARE PROGRESSIVE NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDER PROMPTING ICU ADMISSION
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Lung Cancer Case Report Posters 17 SESSION TYPE: Case Report Posters PRESENTED ON: 10/09/2023 02:10 pm - 02:55 pm INTRODUCTION: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome in the neuromuscular junction associated with several types of cancers, but mostly with small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Symptoms of LEMS can precede signs and symptoms of SCLC by several years, and this may make early diagnosis possible. LEMS and myasthenia gravis (MG) share many clinical features, but unlike MG, LEMS symptoms will improve with muscle use but will have minimal responses to acetylcholinesterase inhibitor administration. We present a case in which the progressive worsening proximal quadriparesis which led to mechanical intubation resulted in the evaluation for lung malignancy in the ICU setting. CASE PRESENTATION: A 62-year-old woman with DM type 2, hepatitis B and C, tobacco, methamphetamine use, and pulmonary nodules was admitted for worsening bilateral leg weakness after a near ground level fall. Associated symptoms were dyspnea, cough, 20 pound weight loss in 3 months. Patient was found to be tachycardic, hypotensive, febrile, with increased respiratory distress and oxygen demand. Neurological exam showed symmetric proximal fatigability with preserved distal strength and subtle left ptosis with fatigability on upward gaze. Initial work up included negative ANA, Anti-Jo, Anti-Smith, CCP, and RF. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed an acute pulmonary embolus within the proximal right upper lobe pulmonary and a right hilar mass. The patient's weakness progressed, and she became hypercapnic and was subsequently intubated. Patient was started on pulse steroids, IV IgG and Mestinon due to suspicious for possible myasthenia crisis.Bronchoscopy with biopsy was done, and this showed extrinsic compression of the right mainstem bronchus, bronchus intermedius, and posterior segment of the right upper lobe likely due to mass effect. Endobronchial ultrasound showed enlarged lymph nodes at stations 7, 11R/mass and 11L. Transbronchial needle aspiration from station 11R/mass was positive for small cell carcinoma. Acetylcholinesterase antibody and MUSK results were negative. A positive voltage gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibody established the diagnosis of Lambert Eaton, and the patient was then started on amifampridine. DISCUSSION: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer in the United States. It accounts for a quarter of all cancer deaths. Based on histology, lung cancers are classified as small cell lung cancers and non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC). SCLC comprises about 15% of lung cancers, while NSCLC comprises approximately 85%. Paraneoplastic LEMS is typically associated with SCLC. This syndrome is characterized by proximal muscle weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and areflexia. The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of P/Q-type VGCC antibodies along with electrodiagnostic studies. Since LEMS is strongly related with malignancy, the diagnosis of LEMS should prompt an immediate and extensive search for underlying cancer. A CT of the chest is the initial recommended imaging study. If the initial evaluation is negative, screening for cancer should continue every 3 to 6 months for at least 2 years. CONCLUSIONS: A prompt diagnosis of LEMS may lead to the early detection of SCLC, as the clinical symptoms of LEMS usually precede cancer detection. Although SCLC has poor prognosis, early detection and treatment can significantly improve patient outcomes. title: SEVERE CASE OF RHABDOMYOLYSIS WITHOUT NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME REQUIRING HEMODIALYSIS FOLLOWING INTRAMUSCULAR CHLORPROMAZINE ADMINISTRATION
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Pharamacotherapeutics Case Report Posters 1 SESSION TYPE: Case Report Posters PRESENTED ON: 10/09/2023 02:10 pm - 02:55 pm INTRODUCTION: Antipsychotics associated rhabdomyolysis is rare but has been reported. Here, we present a rare case of intramuscular (IM) chlorpromazine causing rhabdomyolysis without neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). CASE PRESENTATION: 44-year-old male with history of Prader-Willi syndrome with associated intellectual disability, nonverbal at baseline and impulse control disorder on oral chlorpromazine initially presented for small bowel obstruction. His course was complicated with hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation secondary to aspiration pneumonia. Over the next few days in the ICU, he was found to have worsening kidney function eventually requiring hemodialysis. There was also a concern for seizure like activity after patient had an unwitnessed fall couple of days later. Therefore, further work up was initiated including CT head and EEG which were negative. Patient was evaluated by neurology and ruled out for seizures based on clinical presentation and rest of the work up. However, the patient's Creatinine Kinase (CK) came back elevated at 23,993 which was consistent with rhabdomyolysis and likely the underlying etiology for his renal failure requiring hemodialysis. His physical exam was unremarkable for any compartment syndrome. NMS was also considered as one of the differentials since the patient had a onetime fever of 38.6 °C and new onset renal failure in the setting of rhabdomyolysis on antipsychotics but was ruled out due to lack of muscle rigidity or hemodynamic instability. On further investigation it was noted that his oral chlorpromazine 100mg QID was changed to 50mg IM q6h after intubation. His rhabdomyolysis was thought to be secondary to his antipsychotic as the patient had been receiving IM chlorpromazine for three days, which led to renal failure requiring hemodialysis. Of note, his initial CK was at 353 and creatinine was at baseline which worsened to 6.3 after receiving IM chlorpromazine. His creatine, CK and urine output improved drastically once his medication was switched back to oral and he was successfully transitioned off hemodialysis. DISCUSSION: Rhabdomyolysis is not a well-understood adverse effect of antipsychotic use. The proposed mechanism is involvement of serotoninergic and/or dopaminergic blockade [1]. Another proposed mechanism is increased release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle cells leading to increased muscle contractility and rigidity, breakdown of muscle, and hyperthermia [2]. Our patient did not meet criteria for NMS and there have been previous case reports of antipsychotics causing rhabdomyolysis without NMS, but they have mostly been with haloperidol [4]. This patient is unique as he received chlorpromazine and did not have any compartment swelling at the site of IM injections. The exact mechanism of injury remains unclear, but any form of muscle damage can lead to rhabdomyolysis. Therefore, we suspect that a combination of injury from the IM injections and chlorpromazine induced dopaminergic blockade led to this unique presentation of rhabdomyolysis without NMS. CONCLUSIONS: Our case highlights that IM antipsychotic use can lead to rhabdomyolysis without the rest of clinical findings associated with NMS. Early recognition of this adverse effect is crucial to improve patient outcomes. REFERENCE #1: Packard K, Price P, Hanson A. Antipsychotic Use and the Risk of Rhabdomyolysis. Journal of Pharmacy Practice. 2014;27(5):501-512. doi:10.1177/0897190013516509 REFERENCE #2: Berman BD. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: a review for neurohospitalists. title: PLEURAL EFFUSION DUE TO IGG4-RELATED DISEASE: A UNICORN AMONG HORSES
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Varied Causes of Pleural Effusions SESSION TYPE: Rapid Fire Case Reports PRESENTED ON: 10/11/2023 09:40 am - 10:25 am INTRODUCTION: Etiology of exudative effusion is vast and often remains obscure despite extensive work up. Here we present an unusual cause of pleural effusion. CASE PRESENTATION: 63 year old male presented with rapid enlargement of an inguinal hernia, associated with dysuria and acute urinary retention. CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a large left inguinal hernia containing colon, small bowel and urinary bladder, without associated obstruction and an incidental moderate right pleural effusion with pleural thickening and basilar consolidation of uncertain chronicity. The patient denied pulmonary or constitutional symptoms. He reported a 30 pack year smoking history, having quit more than 15 years ago. He also reported an intentional 40lb weight loss in the preceding 6 months with lifestyle modifications. CT chest revealed a large right pleural effusion with pleural thickening and nodularity predominantly on the right, airspace disease in the right more than left lung and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Patient subsequently underwent thoracentesis, draining 1350 cc of yellow clear fluid. Pleural fluid analysis was consistent with exudative effusion, with negative cytology for malignancy. He subsequently underwent image guided needle biopsy of the pleura, and later an open inguinal hernia repair. Histopathology of pleural and transected hernial sac demonstrated fibroadipose tissue with dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates in a nodular and interstitial pattern separated by thick bands of fibrosis, and increased number of IgG4 plasma cells. Molecular studies for immunoglobulin heavy chain gene rearrangement by PCR showed no clonality. Subsequent blood work revealed normal renal function and calcium levels, and a significant elevation of serum IgG and IgG4 levels (1109 mg/dl). Evaluation for other connective tissue diseases including rheumatoid factor, ANA, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. After multi-specialty consultation with rheumatology, the decision was made not to initiate immunosuppressive therapy albeit a very high IgG4 level due to paucity of symptoms. DISCUSSION: IIgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition that can affect multiple organs. The case presented is an unusual presentation of IgG4 disease with pleural involvement and abdominal involvement with hernia. The pulmonary manifestations of IgG4-RD may mimic sarcoidosis. The hallmarks of IgG4-RD are dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrations with a predominance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in the affected tissue, usually accompanied by some degree of fibrosis and often by obliterative phlebitis and an increased number of eosinophils. Although the pathogenesis of IgG4-RD is poorly understood, there is a growing body of evidence that indicates an antigen-driven process requiring T-cell and B-cell interaction. Steroid is the first line treatment. In a randomized controlled trial conducted by Masamune et al showed that maintaining patients on 5 to 7.5 mg prednisolone for 3 years was effective at reducing relapse rates when compared with steroid taper and cessation. Despite the relative efficacy of this strategy, 1 in 4 patients relapsed while on steroid maintenance. Immunosuppressive therapy can be considered as an auxiliary strategy when there is poor disease control. CONCLUSIONS: Pleural involvement in IgG4-RRD is rare. A high index of suspicion necessary to diagnose IgG4-RD when encountered with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in pleural biopsy. title: HYPERCALCEMIA AND ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY SECONDARY TO RENAL SARCOIDOSIS: COMMON PRESENTATION WITH AN UNCOMMON CAUSE
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Pulmonary Potpourri: Rarest of the Rare SESSION TYPE: Rapid Fire Case Reports PRESENTED ON: 10/10/2023 09:40 am - 10:25 am INTRODUCTION: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease involving multiple systems with varied presentations ranging from asymptomatic to life threatening. Due to this, several patients require extensive workup before a diagnosis can be established. We present a case of severe renal failure and symptomatic hypercalcemia secondary to sarcoidosis. CASE PRESENTATION: A 33-year-old incarcerated male with a past medical history of asthma and anxiety presented to the hospital with a one-month history of dizziness, lightheadedness, visual floaters and an unintentional weight loss of 15 to 20 pounds over the past three months. Review of systems was negative for shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, skin rashes, urinary/rectal bleeding, and focal weakness. At the time of presentation, he was afebrile, with a heart rate of 80 beats per minute with multiple premature ventricular contractions on telemetry, a blood pressure of 115/60 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute saturating at a 100% on room air. Physical examination showed a young adult in no acute distress with a normal cardiovascular, neurological, abdominal and respiratory examination. Prehospital labs showed a creatinine of 4.67 mg/dL, serum calcium level of 11.8 mg/dL, and a hemoglobin of 8.3 g/dL. Initial laboratory work up confirmed the prehospital labs and additionally showed 2+ blood and +1 protein in the urinalysis. Random urine sodium was 43, urine protein to creatinine ratio was 50.30mg/69mg (1.372 mg/mg). Further workup revealed a normal parathyroid hormone level of 13.0 pg/dL, a normal serum protein electrophoresis but elevated angiotensin converting enzyme level of 175.5 u/L. A computed tomography (CT) guided bone marrow biopsy performed to assess for hematological malignancies was negative. CT imaging of the chest showed minimal mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) was significant for enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes at stations 11R, 4R, 7, and 11L. EBUS guided transbronchial needle aspiration was significant for noncaseating granulomas (see figure). A preliminary diagnosis of sarcoidosis was made, and the patient was started on steroids with subsequent improvement of hypercalcemia and renal function. Renal biopsy that was subsequently performed showed chronic, severe, active tubular interstitial nephritis without granulomas but with calcium phosphate deposits, with greater than 60% interstitial fibrosis. DISCUSSION: Clinically evident interstitial nephritis is a rare finding in sarcoidosis and according to observational studies only accounts for 0.7-4.3% of the cases.[1] It is even rarer for a patient to present with acute kidney injury and be diagnosed with sarcoidosis without evidence of respiratory symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: This case highlights the importance of viewing sarcoidosis as a multisystem disease with a myriad of presentations. REFERENCE #1: Sève P, Pacheco Y, Durupt F, et al. Sarcoidosis: A clinical overview from symptoms to diagnosis. Cells. 2021;10(4):766. doi:10.3390/cells10040766 DISCLOSURES: No relevant relationships by Rimsha Ali No relevant relationships by Christopher Franz No relevant relationships by Taaha Mirza

title: HYPERAMMONEMIC ENCEPHALOPATHY IN PATIENT WITH MULTIPLE MYELOMA
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Critical Care Case Report Posters 44 SESSION TYPE: Case Report Posters PRESENTED ON: 10/10/2023 09:40 am - 10:25 am INTRODUCTION: Multiple myeloma (MM) is ranked the second most common hematological malignancy having 1 in 143 lifetime risk and 47% 5 year survival rate. Altered mental status in patient with multiple myeloma could signify hypercalcemia or deranged renal status or hyperammonemia. MM induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy is a rare finding, as the later typically present with hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia and bone lesions. The mechanism of hyperammonemia in this setting is still unclear. Here we present a case of an 81year old male diagnosed with multiple myeloma who had received first course of VRD regimen (Velcade AKA bortezonib, Revlinid AKA lenalidomide and Dexamethasome) prior to admission who presented with altered mental status with hyperammonemic encephalopathy and having persistence raised ammonia level despite measures to reduce the metabolite. CASE PRESENTATION: Our patient is an 81year old male with history of multiple myeloma, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, diabetic retinopathy. He was intubated due to respiratory failure in the setting of altered mental status. Family reported patient having reduced oral intake, excessive fatigue, and multiple episodes of falls in the past month. Patient had received first course of chemotherapy for Multiple myeloma with VRD regimen. He was on Xarelto for atrial fibrillation.Vitals revealed fever (101.5F), bp 111/67mmHg, pulse rate 58, respiratory rate 19, SPO2 100%. Lab findings showed serum creatinine 3.0 (baseline 1.84), INR 1.87, total protein 14mg/dl. His serum calcium was elevated (14mg/dl), he was given calcitonin followed by multiple sessions of hemodialysis, with no improvement in his mental status. He was given a unit of transfusion for haemoglobin level of 6.7g/dl. A trend of persistent elevated serum ammonia was observed despite institution of treatment with lactulose at 30g 6hourly. Notwithstanding all these measures, he remained unweanable from mechanical ventilation until his family requested for compassionate extubation. DISCUSSION: To diagnose multiple myeloma, clinical, laboratory and radiographic assessment is required. It can present with wide range of symptoms with most patient often presenting with fatigue, weight loss and bone pain. Plasma-cell proliferation results in skeletal destruction with osteolytic lesions, anemia, and hypercalcemia. Hyperammonemic encephalopathy in MM is rare and the exact mechanism is poorly understood. The persisted elevated ammonia levels despite treatment suggest a self-sustaining mechanism that need further study to be clearly elucidated. Therapeutic options for treatment of hyperammonemia is directed towards reduction of ammoniagenesis and absorption in gastrointestinal tract, alternatively, treatment with N-carbamylglutamate or supplementation of urea cycle intermediates and glutamine synthesis. Lactulose is considered as first-line therapy for patients with hyperammonemia. Hyperammonemia induced encephalopathy is believed to be due to ammonia conversion to glutamine in astrocyte, resulting in osmotic gradient causing cerebral edema and an increase in intracranial pressure therefore encephalopathy ensues. CONCLUSIONS: Multiple myeloma induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy is rare, however, there is increasing evidence of its possibility. Regardless of the other common cause of altered mental status, the possibility of hyperammonemia should not be undermined. The outcome of management is usually unrewarding, therefore patient with multiple myeloma required close monitoring and aggressive chemotherapy to prevent onset of hyperammonemia. title: CHRONIC MYELOMONOCYTIC LEUKEMIA (CMML) PRESENTING WITH SPONTANEOUS LYSIS TUMOR SYNDROME: A CASE REPORT
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Critical Care Case Report Posters 25 SESSION TYPE: Case Report Posters PRESENTED ON: 10/09/2023 02:10 pm - 02:55 pm INTRODUCTION: Lysis-tumor-syndrome is an oncology-metabolic emergency associated mostly with solid tumors; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common. However, spontaneous-lysis-tumor-syndrome (SLTS), as the initial presentation of acute leukemia, is a rare disorder. CASE PRESENTATION: We present a 76-year-old female with a history of hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis on home-oxygen (O2) at 2-3 liters; she presented complaining of pressure-like chest pain radiating down from the neck, worsening baseline dyspnea, and sharp pain on swallowing, which started three days before admission. She denies fever, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss, or other symptoms. At arrival, her vital signs were unremarkable, besides needing O2 to maintain adequate saturation of 94%. While in the emergency department, the patient developed hypotension of 87/56mmHg, which resolved with 500 mL of normal saline. Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus tachycardia with nonspecific T wave changes, but troponins were consecutively normal twice.Furthermore, initial blood work demonstrated leukocytosis with a white cell blood count (WBC) of 49K with an increase in immature-granulocyte; renal function and liver function were normal. Chest X-ray (CXR) showed chronic fibrotic findings; however, due to the concern of possible ongoing infection, she was started on antibiotics, but all cultures were later negative. Peripheral-blood-smear showed an increased number of WBC's with numerous monocytes, some atypical appearing, rare monocytic blasts with high nucleo-cytoplasm ratio and visible nucleoli, increased number of neutrophils, also some bands, metamyelocytes, and myelocytes, numerous nucleated red blood cells with dysplastic budding nuclei, moderate poikilocytosis, moderate polychromasia, decreased number of platelets with frequently large platelets. Therefore a bone marrow biopsy was performed. However, 12 hours after admission, her creatinine increased from 1.0 mg/dl to 2.4 mg/dl, with worsening respiratory status that needed to escalate O2 therapy to a high-flow-nasal cannula associated with jugular venous distention and chest pain. Subsequently, EKG showed diffuse ST segment elevation in all 12 leads; an echocardiogram showed pericarditis without signs of cardiac tamponade. A new CXR showed pulmonary congestion. Hence the patient was started on diuretics and colchicine.Eighteen hours after admission, the creatinine worsened to 2.5-mg/dl, uric-acid was 11-mg/dl (previously normal), and LDH was 1055-UI/L, phosphorus of 9.8-mg/dl, respectively calcium was 7.8-mg/dl (corrected with albumin), and potassium was 6.5-mEq/L. Therefore, SLTS was diagnosed. Nephrology was contacted to start appropriate treatment; however, the patient further decompensated and died after 20 hours after admission. Bone marrow biopsy results confirmed CMML in the blastic-phase. DISCUSSION: SLTS is a rare entity; our patient met the clinical and symptomatic criteria for SLTS in the context of CMML in a blastic phase which most likely triggered the SLTS. SLTS is caused by the burden and metabolization of the cancer cells, and without treatment, this can be fatal like it was with our patient, who unfortunately died not even 24 hours after admission. Treatment of SLTS is aimed at preventing hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia avoiding cardiac arrhythmias, and if needed, renal replacement therapy. CONCLUSIONS: SLTS is a rare entity; however, high suspicious should be maintained and appropriate treatment instituted even with clinical suspicion because outcomes tend to be fatal REFERENCE #1: Howard SC, Jones DP, Pui CH. title: A CASE OF LAMBERT-EATON MYASTHENIC SYNDROME AND SYNDROME OF INAPPROPRIATE ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE SECRETION AS THE INITIAL PRESENTATION OF SMALL-CELL LUNG CANCER
abstract: SESSION TITLE: Paraneoplastic Syndromes and Immunotherapy Complications SESSION TYPE: Rapid Fire Case Reports PRESENTED ON: 10/11/2023 09:40 am - 10:25 am INTRODUCTION: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a neuroendocrine tumor occurring predominantly in smokers and represents about 15% of all lung cancers. It is often associated with paraneoplastic syndromes caused by ectopic hormone production or immune-mediated tissue destruction by neural antigen expression from neoplastic cells. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) and Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) are examples of paraneoplastic syndromes individually accompanied by SCLC, although the simultaneous occurrence of the two is rare. We present a case of two concurrent paraneoplastic syndromes, LEMS and SIADH as the initial presentation of SCLC. CASE PRESENTATION: A 62-year-old male with a history of active smoking and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with worsening lower extremity weakness and unintentional twenty-pound weight loss for the past few months. Physical exam revealed bilateral lower extremity proximal muscle weakness and hyporeflexia. He was hemodynamically stable, and his labs were normal except for mild hyponatremia of 133mmol/L on presentation. Imaging showed a malignant mediastinal mass, pulmonary nodules/fibrosis, and metastatic liver lesions. Carcinoembryonic antigen was markedly elevated (104ng/mL) which was highly suspicious for primary lung cancer. Lactate dehydrogenase, alpha-fetoprotein, and beta-human chorionic antigen were normal. On day 4, he developed worsening hyponatremia (127mmol/L) with urine studies consistent with SIADH. On day 9, he underwent endobronchial ultrasound bronchoscopy despite significantly reduced negative inspiratory force (NIF) of –25mbar (NIF <-30mbar indicates a high probability of successful ventilator weaning) and vital capacity (VC) of 2L (normal 3-5L). Further work-up revealed positive anti-voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibodies (>400pmol/L), negative acetylcholine receptor antibodies, normal creatinine kinase, and aldolase. He was started on pyridostigmine, steroids, and plasmapheresis on day 13. Subsequently, pathology confirmed SCLC and he was initiated on carboplatin and etoposide. The patient clinically improved and was discharged with close oncology follow up. DISCUSSION: The estimated 5-year survival in metastatic SCLC is 3%. LEMS is present in 1-3% and SIADH in 15% of patients with SCLC at presentation but it is extremely rare for two paraneoplastic syndromes to be present simultaneously on initial presentation. LEMS is characterized by proximal muscle weakness, decreased deep tendon reflexes and bulbar/autonomic dysfunction due to a reduction in the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic vesicles because of anti-VGCC antibodies. LEMS is almost always associated with malignancy, especially SCLC. Our patient had significantly reduced NIF and VC which corresponded with his LEMS severity which is important to consider as cases have been reported where LEMS presented as isolated respiratory failure. Muscle weakness in our patient was further augmented by hyponatremia from SIADH which is a significantly poor prognostic marker in SCLC. Pyridostigmine, steroids and plasmapheresis are guided towards improving initial symptoms, but paraneoplastic syndromes tend to improve as chemotherapy is initiated hence early treatment with carboplatin/etoposide was initiated during hospitalization to improve clinical outcome for our patient. CONCLUSIONS: Early recognition of malignancy, especially SCLC, with multiple paraneoplastic syndromes can lead to prompt treatment initiation for better prognostic results. REFERENCE #1: Gandhi L, Johnson BE. Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with small cell lung cancer. J Natl Compr Canc Netw. 2006 Jul;4(6):631-8. doi: 10.6004/jnccn.2006.0052. PMID: 16813730.
